source.title: Language Models Implement Simple Word2Vec-style Vector Arithmetic
source.authors: Jack Merullo; Carsten Eickhoff; Ellie Pavlick

page_placements.theme: ICL that copying can't explain runs through FFNs, other subspaces or non-induction heads

record.tranche_reason: The study does not test induction heads, but its own FFN-ablation results bear on V6 by distinguishing abstractive in-context retrieval from answering when the answer is present in context, and identifying a role for FFNs in the former.
record.gate_note: The paper mentions induction heads only as a possible explanation for copying an argument token. It does not identify, measure, add, or remove induction heads, nor test their formation or timing. Its FFN-ablation results on extractive and abstractive in-context tasks bear on V6. The intervention results with extracted FFN vectors and zero-shot performance are not results about induction heads or the V6 comparison, so they are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study never identifies, measures or ablates induction heads or any individual attention head. It ablates FFN sublayers on one-shot extractive and abstractive tasks. That shows FFNs matter for recalling answers from pretraining memory but not for copying answers from context. It does not show whether few-shot task learning runs through induction heads or through other heads, which is what V6 names. Induction heads appear only as a speculative possibility in Appendix C, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that FFNs apply additive, Word2Vec-like function updates for recall from pretraining memory (one-to-one relations only), while attention handles copying from local context. The suggestion that induction or mover heads copy the argument is explicitly speculative (Appendix C).
record.recipe_differences: The study uses early decoding and FFN-subnetwork ablations to examine in-context task performance; it does not use the induction-head identification, training-curve, or loss-by-token measurements of the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome varies with whether the answer is available in the prompt (extractive) or must be recalled from pretraining memory (abstractive).

fits_no_version.finding: Across GPT2 sizes, GPT-J and Bloom, removing FFN sublayers from the top sharply cuts one-shot abstractive accuracy. Extractive accuracy, where the answer is in context, degrades much more slowly. Example: Bloom colored objects, extractive -17% vs abstractive -73% (to 1%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mid-to-late FFNs carry in-context tasks that need recall from pretraining memory; tasks answerable by copying from context are largely FFN-independent.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The study does not directly test induction heads or identify which attention heads carry the extractive behaviour. Ablation results are shown largely in figures without uncertainty estimates; the text gives exact ablation percentages for only the Bloom colored-objects example.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant FFN-ablation task/model conditions were left out. Other FFN-vector intervention and zero-shot results were omitted because they do not test the induction-head claims or the V6 comparison.

untested.parts: All; no induction or previous-token heads identified.
All; no loss-by-token-index or head-level attribution.
All; induction behaviour not measured in any model.
All; no data or training manipulation.
Role of induction heads versus other heads in few-shot learning. Only FFN sublayers are ablated; no attention heads are.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 link and labels are removed. FFN ablation cannot show whether induction heads or other heads carry few-shot learning, and the 'reversed' states had no coherent reference to V6. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Whether induction heads form by composing with previous-token heads or implement the specified copying circuit.
Training-time emergence, abruptness, loss-curve bump, and timing relative to in-context-learning gains.
Whether induction heads carry most loss-based in-context learning in large transformers.
Induction behaviour across model families, sizes, runs, architectures, or modalities.
Whether training data or setup changes induction-head formation or the persistence of induction-based in-context learning.

The paper tests FFN ablation on selected in-context tasks, but does not ablate induction heads or other individual heads, measure repeated-token copying, or establish that the tested tasks represent few-shot task learning generally.
Whether induction-head formation comprises multiple sub-steps or overlapping training transitions.

tranche.reason: FFN ablations and vector interventions test argument-function processing, without identifying or measuring induction heads or testing any listed induction-head claim version.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Extractive accuracy is reported as more robust to FFN removal than abstractive accuracy, consistent with local-context retrieval using mechanisms other than FFNs (R1, R3, R5, R7, R9, R11, R13, R15, R17, R19, R21, R23).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: Abstractive accuracy falls more sharply when FFNs are removed; for Bloom's colored-objects task it falls 73%, to 1%, indicating an important FFN role in these tested retrieval tasks (R2, R4, R6, R8, R10, R12, R14, R16, R18, R20, R22, R24).
